title: How To Give Your Students Hope
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In a more personal, reflective piece, Linsin describes shifting his pandemic-era teaching toward deliberately 'drenching' students in hope while still holding them to his usual standards and classroom management plan. Rather than offering a specific strategy or script, he describes an atmosphere he cultivates: sharing his own small joys, simple pleasures, humor, and future plans as a way of modeling that a positive, determined life is possible despite hardship. He is candid that this posture takes real effort on hard days, describing pausing to breathe and imagine himself in his students' shoes before class. He frames the underlying goal as guiding students through uncertainty by convincing them that hope exists even when it isn't immediately visible.
points: Continue enforcing normal classroom management standards even while emphasizing emotional support — the two aren't in conflict.
Model hope concretely by sharing your own small joys, humor, and future plans rather than delivering generic pep talks.
Reorient students toward simple pleasures as an antidote to the loss of purpose caused by prolonged isolation.
Acknowledge frustration and sadness honestly rather than only projecting positivity.
On hard days, deliberately pause to breathe and imagine the crisis from students' perspective before teaching.
quotes: With students experiencing profound mental health struggles because of the pandemic, I’ve taken a different approach to teaching this year.
After all, Covid or not, children need purpose. They need direction and responsibility and a metaphorical kick in the pants.
Since the start of school, I’ve drenched my students in a downpouring of hope. In the midst of so much uncertainty, fear, and isolation, I believe it’s our primary duty as teachers.
I reorient them toward simple pleasures, those that must be savored, appreciated, and cultivated or else will die dry and withering upon the vine.
So I sit and I breathe. I close my eyes and prepare for class by thinking of them, my students, and what it must be like in their shoes—confused, lonely, life on hold.
It’s my job now to guide them through, to help them navigate the forest dark. To convince them that though we can’t see the light, it’s there.
